diseases.name: Anthracnose Fruit Rot
diseases.description: A fungal ripe rot of blueberries that shows as the fruit ripens or after picking.
diseases.causes: The fungus overwinters on twigs and buds; rain splashes spores onto green berries, which stay symptomless until they ripen.
symptoms: Sunken, softening berries at the blossom end
Orange to salmon spore masses on the berries
Berries shrivel; rot spreads in stored fruit
diseases.effect: Ripe fruit rots on the bush and in storage.
diseases.untreated: Losses grow each wet year as the fungus builds up on the twigs.

steps.title: Remove rotting berries
steps.instruction: Pick off rotting berries when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Pick often and cool quickly
steps.instruction: Harvest ripe fruit promptly and chill it.
steps.rationale: Rot develops fast in warm, ripe fruit.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

lifecycle: Spores overwinter on twigs and buds.
Rain splashes them onto green berries.
Infection stays hidden until the fruit ripens.
Ripe berries soften and ooze orange spores.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: blueberry anthracnose

diseases.name: Botrytis Blight
diseases.description: Grey mould of blueberry blossoms, young shoots and fruit.
diseases.causes: Cool, wet weather at bloom; the fungus lives on dead plant matter and its spores are everywhere in the air.
symptoms: Blossoms turn brown and stick together
Grey, fuzzy mould on blossoms and berries
diseases.effect: Blighted flowers set no fruit, and berries rot.
diseases.untreated: Fruit is lost in wet springs and in storage.

steps.title: Remove blighted blossoms and twigs
steps.instruction: Pick off blighted blossoms and twigs when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Improve air movement
steps.instruction: Prune to open the bush and control weeds round it.
steps.rationale: Grey mould needs still, humid air.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide at bloom on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

prevention.title: Avoid excess nitrogen
prevention.detail: Soft growth is more easily infected.

lifecycle: The fungus lives on dead plant matter.
Spores land on blossoms in cool, wet weather.
Flowers brown and grow grey fuzz.
Mould spreads to fruit and shoots.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: blueberry botrytis blight

diseases.name: Mummy Berry
diseases.description: A fungal disease that withers shoots in spring and turns the berries into hard, grey 'mummies'.
diseases.causes: Mummified berries on the ground grow small cup fungi in spring; their spores blight young shoots, which then infect the flowers.
symptoms: Young leaves and shoots wilt and turn brown ('shoot strike')
Infected berries turn cream to pink, then shrivel
Hard, grey, pumpkin-shaped mummies drop to the ground
diseases.untreated: Mummies on the ground start the next spring's epidemic.

steps.title: Pick up mummies
steps.instruction: Rake up or bury the fallen mummies before spring.
steps.rationale: Each mummy produces spores for the next season.

steps.title: Cultivate or mulch under bushes
steps.instruction: Disturb the soil or add fresh mulch in early spring.
steps.rationale: Buries the mummies so the cup fungi cannot release spores.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide at bud break on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

prevention.title: Watch for shoot strike in spring
prevention.detail: It shows the disease is present.

lifecycle: Mummies on the ground grow cup fungi in spring.
Their spores blight young shoots.
Spores from the shoots infect the flowers.
Berries become mummies and drop.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: blueberry mummy berry

diseases.name: Blueberry Leaf Rust
diseases.description: A rust fungus of blueberry leaves; hemlock is its alternate host.
diseases.causes: Spores blow from nearby hemlocks or infected bushes; warm, humid weather lets them infect.
symptoms: Small yellow spots on the upper leaf, turning reddish-brown
Early leaf drop late in the summer
diseases.effect: Bushes lose leaves early, so fewer flower buds form for next year.

steps.title: Remove rusted leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off rusted leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.
steps.rationale: Fewer spores are left to spread.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

lifecycle: Spores blow from hemlocks or infected bushes.
They infect leaves in warm, humid weather.
Yellow spots form, with orange pustules underneath.
New spores spread from bush to bush.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: blueberry rust

diseases.name: Blueberry Scorch
diseases.description: A virus disease that blights blossoms and scorches the leaf edges of highbush blueberry.
diseases.causes: Aphids carry the virus from infected bushes; it also travels in infected cuttings.
symptoms: Blossoms and young leaves die suddenly at flowering
Some varieties only show yellowing or red leaf edges
diseases.effect: Fruit set fails on affected branches.
diseases.untreated: Infected bushes decline over a few years; the virus spreads along the row.

steps.title: Mark and test the bush
steps.instruction: Mark bushes with blossom blight and have a sample tested.
steps.rationale: Frost and other diseases look similar.

steps.title: Remove infected bushes
steps.instruction: Pull out confirmed bushes with their roots.

steps.title: Control aphids
steps.instruction: Keep aphid numbers low as advised locally.

prevention.title: Plant certified virus-tested stock
prevention.detail: Most outbreaks start with infected plants.

prevention.title: Check at every bloom
prevention.detail: Blossom blight is the clearest sign.

lifecycle: Aphids feed on an infected bush.
They carry the virus to healthy bushes.
At bloom, flowers and young leaves die back.
Leaf edges scorch; the bush declines.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: blueberry scorch
